title: Jazz Harmony
intro: Jazz harmony takes the chords of tonal music, adds sevenths, ninths and beyond as normal colour, and organises improvisation around chord symbols and the scales that fit them. The ii–V–I is its basic unit.

blocks.text: In jazz a plain triad sounds unfinished; every chord has at least a seventh (or a sixth on the tonic). A major-key ii–V–I in C is Dm7–G7–Cmaj7; in minor, Dø7–G7(♭9)–Cm6 or Cm(maj7).

The 3rd and 7th of each chord, the guide tones, define its quality, and in a ii–V–I they move by half step or not at all: Dm7's C (7th) falls to B (3rd of G7) while F (3rd) stays as G7's 7th; then G7's F falls to E and B stays as Cmaj7's 7th. A line of guide tones outlines the whole progression in two voices.

widget.title: ii–V–I in C: guide tones, then rootless voicings over a bass

blocks.text: Each chord suggests a scale that contains its chord tones and adds compatible 'tensions':

items: 7 (V): Mixolydian; with altered tensions, the altered scale or half–whole diminished. G7 → G Mixolydian; G7alt → G altered (A♭ melodic minor).
maj7 (I): Ionian, or Lydian to avoid the clash of the 4th with the 3rd. Cmaj7 → C Lydian (F♯).
m7♭5: Locrian or Locrian ♮2. m6 / m(maj7): melodic minor.
Notes a half step above a chord tone are 'avoid notes' that sound like unresolved dissonances when held (F over Cmaj7).

blocks.text: Chord-scale theory (codified at Berklee and in Levine's book) is a practical approximation; many great improvisers think instead in terms of chord tones, approach notes and melody.

A turnaround leads back to the top of a tune: I–vi–ii–V (Cmaj7–A7–Dm7–G7 with A7 as V/ii). 'Rhythm changes' are the chords of Gershwin's 'I Got Rhythm', an AABA form whose A sections are turnarounds and whose bridge is a chain of dominants (III7–VI7–II7–V7) round the circle of fifths.

Learn rootless voicings in two positions for every ii–V–I: left hand only, moving each note to the nearest note of the next voicing. Over a walking bass, the left hand plays these 'comping' chords in short rhythmic figures while the right hand improvises.

items: Reharmonization (#/arts/music-theory/jazz-harmony/reharmonization): tritone substitution, backdoor dominants, Coltrane changes and modal harmony.

blocks.title: ii–V–I
blocks.text: Spell a major ii–V–I in B♭ with sevenths, and give the guide-tone line that starts on B♭, the 7th of the ii chord.
solution: ii7 = Cm7 (C E♭ G B♭), V7 = F7 (F A C E♭), Imaj7 = B♭maj7 (B♭ D F A).

Guide tones alternate 7th and 3rd: B♭ (7th of Cm7) falls a half step to A (3rd of F7), which stays as A (7th of B♭maj7). The other guide-tone line runs E♭ (3rd of Cm7) → E♭ (7th of F7) → D (3rd of B♭maj7).

blocks.title: Chord scale
blocks.text: Which scale fits E♭maj7♯11, and which fits Bø7?
solution: maj7♯11: Lydian, E♭ F G A B♭ C D. ø7: Locrian (B C D E F G A), or Locrian ♮2 (B C♯ D E F G A, 6th mode of D melodic minor).

blocks.text: Sources: Levine, M. (1995). The Jazz Theory Book. Sher Music; Mulholland, J. & Hojnacki, T. (2013). The Berklee Book of Jazz Harmony. Berklee Press; Martin, H. (1996). Charlie Parker and Thematic Improvisation. Scarecrow; Strunk, S. (2002). Harmony (i). In The New Grove Dictionary of Jazz, 2nd ed..
